clue.text: But a solo pianist cannot: succeed like this

definitions.text: But a solo pianist cannot: succeed like this

parts.words: But a solo pianist cannot: succeed like this
parts.note: a pianist needs both hands at the keyboard, yet the phrase also means achieving something alone, unaided

explanation.surface: A remark that a lone performer can win, but not a lone pianist.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for doing something without help literally means using one hand only, which a pianist cannot manage.
explanation.definitionFit: Succeeding alone, without any helper, is the idiom; literally it describes using one hand.

clue.text: Plate lost by an unlucky horse ?

definitions.text: Plate lost by an unlucky horse ?

parts.words: Plate lost by an unlucky horse ?
parts.note: in a race of this kind the winning horse is auctioned afterwards, so even victory loses the owner the horse

explanation.surface: A racehorse unluckily casting a shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plate' suggests a horseshoe; it is a race prize, and in this race the winner is put up for sale.
explanation.definitionFit: A race whose winner must be offered for sale is a kind of plate race.

clue.text: They are knotty little items on the surface

definitions.text: They are knotty little items on the surface

parts.words: They are knotty little items on the surface
parts.note: knotty means knobbly here: small rounded lumps or swellings on skin or a plant

explanation.surface: Tricky small problems that sit on the surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knotty' suggests difficult; it means lumpy, like little knots.
explanation.definitionFit: Small rounded lumps or swellings, as on skin or roots.

clue.text: Hot drink and warm covering

definitions.meaning: an old English drink of hot spiced ale with roasted apples
soft fleece from young sheep, knitted into jumpers

explanation.surface: A cosy night in with a hot drink and a blanket.
explanation.walkthrough: The drink is an old English wassail of hot ale with roasted apple pulp floating like fleece.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine fleece from young sheep warms the body; the same name was given to a hot spiced ale.

clue.text: Trapdoor by which to escape from shelling

definitions.meaning: an opening in a floor or deck closed by a door
a chick emerges by breaking out of its egg

explanation.surface: A trapdoor as the way out during an artillery barrage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shelling' suggests bombardment; it is the eggshell a chick breaks out of.
explanation.definitionFit: A deck or floor opening; also what a chick does emerging from its egg.

clue.text: Falls between Empire State and Commonwealth Nation

definitions.text: Falls between Empire State and Commonwealth Nation

parts.words: Falls between Empire State and Commonwealth Nation
parts.note: the Empire State is New York; the Commonwealth nation is Canada, and famous waterfalls lie on that border

explanation.surface: Something tumbling down between a skyscraper and a country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls' looks like a verb; it is the waterfalls on the New York (the Empire State) and Canada border.
explanation.definitionFit: The great waterfalls straddle the border of New York State and Canada.

clue.text: Black suits her drama character

parts.note: Eugene O'Neill's play Mourning Becomes ... says black mourning clothes suit this Greek heroine

explanation.surface: A remark that dark clothing flatters a theatrical woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The play title Mourning Becomes Electra: 'becomes' means suits, and mourning dress is black. The page prints 'dramatic'.
explanation.definitionFit: O'Neill's play is titled Mourning Becomes Electra, the Greek heroine reworked.

clue.text: Should they have iron lungs ?

parts.note: an iron lung is a breathing machine, but iron links also make a chain, and heavy smokers light one cigarette from the last

explanation.surface: Asking whether certain patients need breathing machines.
explanation.walkthrough: An iron lung is a medical respirator; iron is also what chains are made of, and these smokers go one after another.
explanation.definitionFit: People who smoke cigarettes continuously, lighting each from the previous one.

clue.text: I swore by mine in the old days

definitions.text: I swore by mine in the old days

parts.words: I swore by mine in the old days
parts.note: the archaic oath 'by my ...' invoked a holy relic or sacred thing, so the speaker swore by it

explanation.surface: Someone recalling a favourite thing they once trusted completely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swore by' looks like praise for something trusted; here it is literal, as in the archaic oath 'by my halidom'.
explanation.definitionFit: A halidom is a holy relic or sanctuary, used in old oaths.

clue.text: Kyd's Spanish piece

parts.note: Thomas Kyd, Elizabethan dramatist, wrote a revenge play titled The Spanish ... whose last word is the genre

explanation.surface: A child's Spanish coin or work of art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kyd' reads like 'kid', but it is the playwright Thomas Kyd, whose famous play is The Spanish Tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Kyd's best-known drama, a revenge play, is titled The Spanish Tragedy.

clue.text: Absent-minded U.S. song hero?

parts.note: the American song's hero stuck a feather in his cap and called it macaroni; doodling is aimless scribbling done absent-mindedly

explanation.surface: Asking who the forgetful hero of an American song is.
explanation.walkthrough: A doodle is an idle scribble made absent-mindedly; the hero of the American song is a Yankee.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of a famous American patriotic song.

clue.text: Shakespeare's winter wall-hangings

parts.note: the winter song in Love's Labour's Lost opens 'When ... hang by the wall', so these are frozen spikes hanging from walls

explanation.surface: Tapestries decorating a playwright's house in winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wall-hangings' suggests tapestries; it is the song in Love's Labour's Lost beginning 'When icicles hang by the wall'.
explanation.definitionFit: Frozen drips hang from walls in the winter song of Love's Labour's Lost.

clue.text: Cheer? The K. 0.'d boxer doesn't

definitions.meaning: to cheer someone is to encourage them
a knocked-out boxer is unconscious, so does not catch the referee's count reaching ten

explanation.surface: Asking whether a beaten fighter can raise a cheer.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the second sense is HEAR TEN: the knocked-out boxer misses the count of ten. The page prints 'K.O.'d'.
explanation.definitionFit: To encourage or cheer someone up; split, the letters say a floored fighter fails to catch the count.

clue.text: Makes a subscription in marks

definitions.meaning: to subscribe is to write one's name below, as one does on a document

explanation.surface: Someone paying a subscription in German currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks' suggests the old German currency; it is symbols or traces, and 'subscription' means writing one's name under something.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing one's name under a document is subscribing; symbols or indications are also this word.

clue.text: Hang a rope out of this institution

indicators.note: out signals the letters of the phrase being knocked out of their order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A grim instruction to hang a rope outside some institution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges HANG A ROPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A home for children without parents is a classic charitable institution.

clue.text: But this plant is not dependent on wind or water

definitions.text: But this plant is not dependent on wind or water

parts.words: But this plant is not dependent on wind or water
parts.note: plant means factory machinery, here a mill driven by an engine rather than a windmill or watermill

explanation.surface: A plant that thrives without wind or water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' suggests a growing thing needing water; it is industrial plant, a mill driven by an engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A mill driven by engine or electricity rather than by sails or a water wheel.

clue.text: Eccentric don in society

definitions.note: describes a member of a friendly society

parts.note: eccentric means odd
a university don is a fellow of a college

explanation.surface: A peculiar university lecturer moving in high society.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oddfellows are a friendly society (a mutual benefit club); a member is one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Oddfellows, a mutual-aid friendly society, belongs to that fraternal organisation.

clue.text: Charged both ways for the aerial

definitions.meaning: having positive and negative electric poles at either end
describes a radio antenna made of two rods fed at the centre

explanation.surface: Billed twice over for a television antenna.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged both ways' suggests paying twice; it is electric charge, positive and negative.
explanation.definitionFit: Having two opposite electric poles; a two-rod antenna takes the same name.

clue.text: Draughts can be simply sickening!

parts.note: draughts are doses of medicine, and some are given to make a patient vomit

explanation.surface: A complaint that a game of draughts, or a cold wind, is nauseating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draughts' suggests the board game or chilly air; it is doses of medicine that induce vomiting.
explanation.definitionFit: Medicines given to make someone vomit.

clue.text: Made into a personal issue by Sir Edward

indicators.note: by here means the letters are supplied by the run of words Sir Edward, which holds them in a row

explanation.surface: A knight named Edward turning a matter into a personal grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Personal issue' suggests a grievance; 'issue' here is offspring, so to make someone one's issue is to father them. The letters run inside 'Sir Edward' (SIR plus ED).
explanation.definitionFit: Fathered offspring; issue means children, so begetting makes someone one's issue.

clue.text: Is Lise a possible victim of European partition ?

indicators.note: possible signals that a possible arrangement of these letters is wanted

explanation.surface: Asking whether a woman called Lise suffered when Europe was carved up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possible' rearranges IS LISE A. The region was divided between Germany, Poland and Czechoslovakia.
explanation.definitionFit: This central European region was repeatedly split between states, notably after both world wars.

clue.text: You'll need another glass to do this!

definitions.text: You'll need another glass to do this!

parts.words: You'll need another glass to do this!
parts.note: glass here is a new pane fitted in a window frame, not a second drink

explanation.surface: A drinker reasoning that another glass is required.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another glass' suggests a second drink; it is a new pane fitted into a window frame. Crossings R, G, A, E fit.
explanation.definitionFit: To fit new panes into a window again.

clue.text: Top job for Josephine

parts.note: Josephine, wife of Napoleon, was crowned to the highest rank a woman could hold in his France

explanation.surface: A woman named Josephine landing a senior post.
explanation.walkthrough: Josephine is Napoleon's wife, crowned Empress of the French in 1804.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon's consort held the female imperial title, the highest rank in his France.

clue.text: Such stockings suggest the need for ladders

definitions.text: Such stockings suggest the need for ladders

parts.words: Such stockings suggest the need for ladders
parts.note: very fine stockings ladder easily, and the same word for a steep cliff calls for ladders to climb it

explanation.surface: Fine stockings that seem bound to ladder.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladder is a run in a stocking; the word also means vertical, like a cliff needing ladders to climb.
explanation.definitionFit: Very thin, see-through hosiery; also perpendicular, as a cliff face.

clue.text: It's pre-Medici, according to Browne

parts.note: Sir Thomas Browne's book title has one Latin word placed before Medici

explanation.surface: A historian dating something to before the Medici family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pre-Medici' looks like a historical period; it means the word before 'Medici' in Sir Thomas Browne's Religio Medici (A Doctor's Religion).
explanation.definitionFit: Browne's seventeenth-century book is titled Religio Medici, Latin for a physician's faith.

clue.text: It causes the old sailor anger-even St. Andrew's cross

parts.note: an old salt is a veteran sailor
ire means anger

explanation.surface: Something enrages a veteran seaman, even the Scottish flag.
explanation.walkthrough: St Andrew's cross is the diagonal cross on Scotland's flag; 'It causes' and 'even' only join.
explanation.definitionFit: The diagonal X-shaped cross of Scotland's patron saint is called this in heraldry.

clue.text: Put in this month's total

parts.note: inst. (instant) is the old business abbreviation for this month
the total is all

explanation.surface: Entering this month's sum in the accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: Old commercial letters wrote 'the 5th inst.' meaning the 5th of this month.
explanation.definitionFit: To fit or put something in place is to set it up for use.

clue.text: How to ring a bell in Fleet Street

definitions.text: How to ring a bell in Fleet Street

parts.words: How to ring a bell in Fleet Street
parts.note: to ring a bell you push and let go; Fleet Street was London's newspaper district, where a statement for journalists is issued

explanation.surface: Directions for sounding a doorbell in a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: Fleet Street was the home of the British national press; to ring a bell you press then release.
explanation.definitionFit: An official statement issued to newspapers; literally a push and let go of a bell button.
